overview: Working memory is the short-term notepad that holds a few items while you use them. IQ tests lean on it in digit spans, sequence recall and multi-step puzzles, so practising it directly lifts your performance across the whole test.

strategy.b: Short-term memory holds about four chunks, not four single items. Turn 4 9 1 7 2 8 into 49, 17 and 28 and the load drops sharply.
Repeat the sequence under your breath while it is on screen. Rehearsal keeps items active until you need them, and the habit carries over to any list you must hold.
Build a quick image or sentence that joins the items in order, such as a cat jumping over a red car. Vivid links are easier to replay than an abstract list.
Ignore background noise and do not check your phone while the list is visible. Attention decides what enters memory at all, so a moment of distraction costs you items.

fig.title: Chunking a long list
fig.note: Groups of two or three are easier to hold.

drills.name: Digit span
drills.how: Read the digits once, then close your eyes and say them back in order, grouping them into pairs or triples as you go. Start with four or five digits and add one whenever you recall a full list correctly.
drills.tip: Say each group aloud in a steady rhythm, the way you would read out a phone number.
drills.mistake: Trying to memorise every digit as a separate item, which overloads memory quickly. Fix it by grouping the digits into threes so you hold three chunks instead of seven loose numbers.

ex.q: The digits 6 2 9 4 are shown for two seconds. Which recall is correct?
ex.why: You must give the digits in the exact order shown, so only 6294 keeps 6, 2, 9 and 4 in sequence.

drills.name: Digit reversal
drills.how: Hear or see a string of digits, then give them back in backwards order without writing them down. Work from the last digit towards the first, one chunk at a time, so you never have to hold the whole list in a flipped state.
drills.tip: Picture the digits on a number line and read them from the right-hand end.
drills.mistake: Reversing the digits in your head before you have fully stored them, which makes you drop one. Fix it by memorising the list forwards first, then reading the last digit and working back.

ex.q: The digits 3 8 5 1 are shown. What is the correct reversed order?
ex.why: Read from the last digit to the first: 1, 5, 8, 3, which gives 1583.

drills.name: Letter span
drills.how: Watch a row of consonants appear, then recall them in the same order. Use consonants so the letters do not form words, and add one more letter to the row each time you succeed.
drills.tip: Say each letter silently in its sound, since the sounds give your memory a second hook.
drills.mistake: Trying to turn the letters into words, which hides the order when the letters are not a real word. Fix it by grouping the consonants into short sound units of two or three letters.

ex.q: The letters H, L, C, V, N appear in that order. Which letter came third?
ex.why: Counting from the start, H is first, L is second and C is third.

drills.name: Word span
drills.how: Hear a list of short, unrelated words, then recall them in the same order. Link each word to the next with a short image or sentence so the list becomes a chain you can walk through.
drills.tip: Build one vivid scene that uses all the words, then walk through it from left to right.
drills.mistake: Remembering the words but not their positions, which loses marks on order-based questions. Fix it by tying each word to a position marker such as first, second or third, then recalling by position.

ex.q: The words apple, river, candle and pencil are heard in that order. Which word came third?
ex.why: Counting in order, apple is first, river is second and candle is third.

drills.name: Long digit span
drills.how: Work with sequences of eight to twelve digits, which are longer than normal capacity. Split the sequence into groups of three, memorise each group as a unit, then join the units in order when you recall them.
drills.tip: Find one simple pattern in each chunk, such as a run of rising or repeating digits, and anchor on it.
drills.mistake: Trying to hold all ten digits at once and losing the middle ones. Fix it by repeating each group aloud before you move on, so each chunk is locked in before you add more.

ex.q: The digits 4 8 2 7 1 9 5 0 3 6 are split into groups of three from the start. Which is the first group?
ex.why: Grouping from the start gives 482, 719, 503 and a final 6, so the first group is 482.

levels: Level 1: Recall three digits in order after a short pause.
Level 2: Recall four or five digits, or three words, in the correct order.
Level 3: Reverse a four-digit string and recall five consonants in order.
Level 4: Recall six or seven digits using groups of three.
Level 5: Recall eight digits or six words in order while a light distraction plays.
Level 6: Recall ten to twelve digits, then reverse part of the list from memory.
routine: Day 1: Spend five minutes on digit span, starting at three digits and adding one after each success.
Day 2: Spend five minutes on digit reversal with four-digit strings, reading the last digit first.
Day 3: Practise letter span with consonants, aiming for five letters recalled in order.
Day 4: Practise word span with four unrelated nouns, linking them into one vivid scene.
Day 5: Attempt a long digit span of ten digits split into threes, then rest and repeat the week.
